text: s are often first-line therapy especially if nasal congestion is a domi- nant feature. The role of antihistamines is more limited; sedating antihistamines are useful in reducing nasal secre- tions because of their antimuscarinic actions; however, non-sedating antihistamines are relatively ineffective. In patients in whom rhinorrhoea is a particular problem, in- tranasal ipratropium is of value. Although intranasal sym- pathomimetics have also been used they should generally be avoided because of the risk of rebound congestion. Oral sympathomimetics are largely ineffective. Other therapies tried include topical capsaicin, to induce local desensitisation, and nasal douching with a saline and sodium bicarbonate solution. References 1. Horak F.
